analysisDescription:
Initial Exploration
To do this, I started off by playing the game and exploring it, joining crews, completing quests, and competing in events. I watched players communicate, collaborate, and dynamically change strategies based on their ongoing performance.

Identifying Collaboration Types
After that, I categorized the forms of collaboration that existed within the game. I listed Free Collaboration because gamers are free to collaborate; no strict rules confine them to inflexible collaboration. I also included Concurrent Collaboration: players collaborate side by side, which happens throughout the game in instances such as when navigating and fighting using ships.

Communications Dynamics
I analyzed the various channels of communications available to the players both in verbal and non-verbal ways. In this, I identified the incorporation of voice chat and emotive since these are the tools that allow for real-time interaction and expression of feelings, hence improving cooperation. I analyzed how these forms of communication influence team dynamics and decision-making.

Dependency Analysis and Player Action
I analyzed the dependencies of player interaction: Spatial Dependencies are crucial for navigating and cooperating with teammates. It requires knowledge of player positioning relative to teammates and the environment in order to execute tasks. I also said how the players create Synergies due to the fact that players individual abilities combine to make one another more effective.

Asymmetry Assessment
Understanding that the capability of character is asymmetric in nature, I examined how various crew roles enable different strategies and manners of cooperating. Asymmetry in this respect provides the opportunity for players to make gains out of their own strengths and, hence, to generate much more dynamic interactions and coordinated efforts toward the realization of mutual goals.

Conclusion and Reflection
By applying the LFCG framework, a whole new angle of analysis that put serious focus on the cooperative gameplay and communication of Sea of Thieves with an emphasis on player interdependencies emerged. This has not just added depth to my understanding of the game but also suggested the ways in which cooperative dynamics enrich the experience of players in multiplayer settings. Overall, the context therefore makes this game a highly potent case study to see the working of the principles of cooperative learning and interaction in a game environment.
frameworkComments: The LFCG framework emphasizes players agency and dynamism in interaction during cooperation in Sea of Thieves. For this reason, the game allows flexibility in players choosing roles and strategies. However, it still lacks the balance of competition and cooperation, and the strong inclusion of diversity within the interaction of its players.

dimensionExamples.example: This may happen with other crews on the open world, or vice versa, in unplanned ways and may result in unexpected interactions, having possibilities of temporary alliances or outright conflicts.

dimension.title: Serendipitous
dimension.description: Serendipitous formation happens in games where groups are not defined structures and the gameplay itself (typically proximity) is used to group players.

dimensionExamples.example: Players can form a crew with their friends or any other players they know, creating a team with established roles and functions that make cooperation easier when completing certain tasks.

dimension.title: Party Creation
dimension.description: Party Creation encompasses all games where groups are defined by the players themselves prior to initiating gameplay, typically leveraging friend lists or co-located party creation.

dimensionExamples.example: The Sea of ​​Thieves does not pause the ongoing session when a player joins or leaves it. It maintains the continuity of missions and activities even in a multiplayer scenario where a session might endure for all sorts of time. If a player needs to leave, another replaces him, and the team goes on with normality.

dimension.title: Drop-in/Drop-out
dimension.description: Drop-in/Drop-out encompasses games where there is the ability for players to join in the midst of the gameplay and drop out at any point.

dimensionExamples.example: It also includes an in-game "Looking for Group" system, which helps the players to either find an open crew or add more players to their own crew. This feature is very useful, especially for players who would like to co-op with other members of the community for mission completion or other challenges like boss fights or PvP against other ships.

dimension.title: Looking for Group
dimension.description: Looking for Group happens when there are grouping mechanisms that allow players to formally look for and create a group/party. This is typically achieved through matchmaking or looking for group queues.

dimensionExamples.example: Most players organize crews among friends or colleagues where some roles are predefined, helmsman, gunner, or navigator. Coordinated groups like this do pop up in more difficult missions, and very often players really plan out specific strategies to make their teams as effective as possible.

dimension.title: Organised Grouping
dimension.description: Organised Grouping covers all features that establish groups/communities (e.g. guilds) within games, which typically persist across different gaming sessions and may have defined roles and/or hierarchy.

dimensionExamples.example:
Missions of teamwork: Examples of such missions are treasure hunt missions and defeating bosses. Players will communicate and cooperate regarding the way to go through challenges, distribution of resources, strategy, and methods to use.
Reward Won: This is where a crew, after winning, is given gold and loot. This would be a way of helping them build more cohesion and the feeling that it was a mission well accomplished.
Social Interactions: Again, there's a sort of cameraderie involved, for often players will form alliances or at least help each other out in random encounters. These, too, make memorable shared experiences since they are fighting another crew or exploring the world.
Alliance Mechanics: Players will be able to temporarily form an alliance with other crews through the sharing of resources and experience points between the two-a further reinforcement of cooperation over individualism.

dimension.title: Shared
dimension.description: Shared goals consist of singular objectives that multiple players pursue and work together to achieve

dimensionExamples.example:
Solo Play: This enables a player to go solo in the ship, undertake voyages, and explore on one's own without relying on the crew. This free-play style will let players take personal approaches to challenges or exploration.
Specialization within a role: A crew can have their members enact very specialized roles, such as those of navigator or gunner. These specialized roles allow the players to become more focused on specific tasks and, in that process, increase their sense of autonomy in how they contribute to the team.
Freedom to Play: A player can play his own game in an individual way, tending to focus either on PvP, exploration, or completing quests. Player independence can lead to a more unique and diverse experience.
Decision and Consequence: Players are presented with personal choices, showing consequences for their own play-for example, whether to fight or flee from combat-which appear to emphasize the idea of autonomy in a shared world.

dimension.title: Independent
dimension.description: Independent goals define individual goals that do not directly interact with other players,  typically different from other players.

dimensionExamples.example:
PvP Encounters: Players engage in battles with other crews, making it a smorgasbord of conflict pitted against each other in racing for resources, treasure, or dominance in the seas. Tensions often may evolve to rivalries as players may need to betray or align themselves with other players to fulfill situational needs.
Resource Competition: In events or treasure hunts, other players have to compete for the same loot; thus, direct conflict over resources. High-stakes scenarios emerge, making cooperation break down.
Moral Dilemmas: These are the situations where players make a certain choice, which may have certain conflicted actions. An example would be if the players needed to either save a sinking ship or take advantage of their situation. This may create tension among the crews or between the players themselves.
Alliances and Betrayals: The dynamic of forming alliances can become so conflicting; hence, later on, players would also be able to betray each other aside from winning an advantage in a race or competition.

dimension.title: Conflicting
dimension.description: Conflicting goals are also observable in some cooperative games, where typically, players compete in certain sections that do not affect the overarching goal of the game. While no semi-cooperative games were observed, in these types of games, conflicting goals can also be mixed with shared goals

dimensionExamples.example: Events within the Community: Seasonal events and challenges often encourage players to cooperate in order to achieve common objectives and help build a sense of community and camaraderie.

dimension.title: Community
dimension.description: Community progression is defined by the joint efforts of players in a larger community (e.g. guilds, factions, or even an entire player base) that, while not necessarily playing together, can contribute to typically shared consequences.

dimensionExamples.example:
Dynamic World: Every server, because of the different people on at any given moment in time, offers different opportunities to encounter, loot, and challenges, which in turn affect how crews make their way through missions.
Server events: These are events that can happen on one or more specific servers; for example, a rare treasure spawns, or a world boss spawns that can affect all the players' progression related to whatever is going on in their server.

dimension.title: Server
dimension.description: Server progression is defined by the existence of persistent mutable worlds that a number of players share. The action of players (i.e. collaborating or not) can impact the overall progression/evolution of the game world, affecting others.

dimensionExamples.example:
Personal goals: The game allows the player to set personal goals, such as leveling up with certain factions, earning cosmetics, or mastering the ways of handling a spaceship in dogfighting.
Solo Play: This allows players to progress alone, accept quests, and learn the world in their own independent way. This allows for more personal experience in a playstyle that fits their preferences.

dimension.title: Individual
dimension.description: Individual progression is defined by individual choice and the individual impact of the progression. In-game activities can vary from individual to fully cooperative but progression affects the individual.

dimensionExamples.example: When players first enter Sea of Thieves, they create their pirate character. They can choose various physical features, such as gender, skin tone, hair style, and clothing, to create a unique avatar. This allows for a personal expression of identity within the shared game world.

dimension.title: Single
dimension.description: Single applies to any game where players have control of one single entity.

dimensionExamples.example: Features and outfits and ships can be combined to create a distinctive pirate. Continual updates, like expressive emotes, bring additional individuality and social functions that will engender an active community and determine how players identify.

dimension.title: Customisation
dimension.description: Customisation applies when players select their identity by creating or modifying (with a certain degree of freedom) the play style of an entity.

dimensionExamples.example: Freedom in an open world grants players the power to tailor experiences through questing, character development, and interaction within a community.

dimension.title: Customisable
dimension.description: Customisable encompasses all games with upgrades, levelling systems, and others that give players the ability to create and modify their representation throughout the game.

dimensionExamples.example: The players are teammates and they need to both cooperate to surpass each stage of the game.

dimension.title: Teammates
dimension.description: Teammates, where players within a team need to coordinate their actions, abilities, and roles in order to reach a common goal against at least another team.

dimensionExamples.example: In the mini-games and ship races, the players engage in some light, friendly competition without disturbing the main storyline of progress within the game.

dimension.title: Competitors
dimension.description: Competitors, where you may be able to compete with other players, either momentarily or through the whole game session (e.g. team vs team match-based games).

dimensionExamples.example: The players interact within the same world.

dimension.title: Shared
dimension.description: Shared world views apply to a game when players have access to the same world.

dimensionExamples.example: The game has the possibility to be played in first person.

dimension.title: Distinct
dimension.description: Distinct refers to when each player has control of their own individual viewpoint, typically through separate screens.

dimensionExamples.example: Players can collaborate with other players or not, the game allows flexibility in teamwork without strict requirements and lots of different scenarios.

dimension.title: Free Collaboration
dimension.description: In free collaboration, players can take on available tasks as they wish and decide how to contribute.

dimensionExamples.example: Players work together simultaneously during the gameplay, like the following examples: navigating, fighting, and completing quests in real-time, enhancing their cooperative experience.

dimension.title: Concurrent Collaboration
dimension.description: In concurrent collaboration, players have to perform gameplay tasks concurrently.

dimensionExamples.example: Effective communication is essential for coordinating actions, strategizing during encounters and achieving objectives.

dimension.title: Required/Incentivised
dimension.description: When Required/Incentivised, the game challenges require players to communicate (e.g. when there is essential asymmetric information), or incentivised through challenges that are made easier through it (e.g. coordinating combined actions for maximum effect).

dimensionExamples.example: Players can use voice chat for real-time coordination and social interaction.

dimension.title: Voice Chat
dimension.description: Support for players to communicate using their voice

dimensionExamples.example: To express feelings or intentions during gameplay.

dimension.title: Emotes
dimension.description: Players can communicate through particular animations their characters have (e.g. pointing at something)

dimensionExamples.example: Players rely on their positions relative to one another and their surroundings as a way of performing tasks efficiently, such as navigation through the process of sailing a ship, engaging in a battle, or exploring an island.

dimension.title: Spatial
dimension.description: Spatial, inspired by Reuter et al. 2014, happens when the game forces or incentivises players to be at a certain distance from one another. This can happen in a variety of ways, for example, by creating a radius around which players cannot trespass or by designing mechanics that punish players that move too far away from the group.

dimensionExamples.example: All characters have different abilities, so players can do different things from their teammates. Characters abilities synergise allowing cooperation between players.

dimension.title: Abilities
dimension.description: Abilities, as described by Harris et al. 2016, are where one player can do things another player cannot. In games where these actions synergise or are complementary, it incentivises collaboration.

dimensionExamples.example: Players' abilities enhance teamwork and navigation skills can combine in synergy for a well-coordinated crew effort.

dimension.title: Synergies
dimension.description: Synergies extended from Rocha et. al 2008 allow one entity to assist or change the game actions (e.g. abilities) of another.
